# The Seasons of Saltcote Marsh

Saltcote Marsh lies on the inner shore of a shallow bay, sheltered from the open sea by a long shingle spit called the Tiller. Behind the spit, the land falls away into a broad, nearly level plain of mud, grass, and winding water. Two small rivers, the Wenn and the Callow, come down from the low chalk hills to the north and lose themselves in the marsh before reaching the bay. Twice each day the tide pushes in through a gap at the eastern end of the Tiller, fills the creeks, spreads across the lower flats, and drains away again. Everything that grows or feeds on Saltcote follows the rhythm of this water and the slower turning of the year.

The marsh was not always shaped as it is now. Some centuries ago the Tiller extended farther west and nearly closed the bay, and the area that is now marsh was a brackish lagoon with reed beds along its edges. Storms gradually broke the spit back to its present length, the tide gained freer entry, and silt carried in from the bay began to settle among the reeds. The reeds gave way to salt-tolerant grasses, and the lagoon filled until only a branching network of creeks remained. In the later period of settlement, farmers built a clay sea wall along the northern margin to claim grazing land, and the ground behind that wall, cut off from the tide, slowly dried into pasture. The wall marks a sharp line between two kinds of country: on one side wet, salt-crusted, and shifting, and on the other green, fenced, and still.

The marsh itself falls into zones according to height. Nearest the bay are the bare mudflats, exposed only at low tide, grey-brown and glistening, and riddled with the burrows of worms and small crustaceans. Above them lies the low marsh, flooded on most tides and colonised by cordgrass and glasswort, the latter a fleshy jointed plant that stores salt water in its swollen stems. Higher still is the middle marsh, where sea lavender, sea aster, and sea purslane form a dense grey-green carpet. At the top, reached only by the highest tides of spring and autumn, is the upper marsh, where sea couch grass and rushes blend into the turf along the foot of the sea wall. Scattered through all of this are salt pans, shallow hollows where seawater is trapped and evaporates in summer, leaving rims of white crystals.

Winter is the season when Saltcote is most crowded with birds. From the late autumn onward, flocks arrive from breeding grounds far to the north and east, where the ground has frozen and food has vanished. Brent geese come in dark, low skeins over the Tiller, calling with a soft guttural murmur, and settle on the flats to graze eelgrass and green algae. When the tide covers their feeding grounds, they move onto the pastures behind the sea wall and crop the winter grass. Wigeon gather in large rafts on the creeks and whistle constantly. Teal, the smallest of the ducks, crowd into the muddy edges of the pools and sift the shallow water with their bills.

The waders are the most numerous winter residents. Dunlin feed in dense, restless flocks along the tide line, probing the soft mud for worms. Knot, plump and grey in their winter plumage, gather in tight bands on the outer flats. Curlew walk the creeks alone or in loose groups, using long down-curved bills to reach lugworms deep in their burrows. Redshank, nervous and quick, give loud piping alarm calls whenever anything moves along the marsh edge. Grey plover stand apart from the others, running a few steps, pausing, and running again as they watch for movement on the surface of the mud. The different lengths and shapes of their bills allow these birds to take prey from different depths, so that one stretch of mud can feed several species at once.

The tide governs their day as much as the light does. As the water rises, the waders are pushed from the lower flats toward the higher ground, and they eventually gather in packed roosts on the shingle of the Tiller or on raised banks within the marsh. There they stand shoulder to shoulder, many with heads tucked under their wings, until the falling tide uncovers the mud again. At these times the flocks sometimes lift into the air together, turning and wheeling so that their pale undersides and darker backs flash alternately against the sky.

Winter weather on Saltcote is raw. Easterly winds sweep across the bay with nothing to stop them, and hard frosts can glaze the upper pools with ice. During the coldest spells the creeks freeze at their margins, the mud stiffens, and feeding becomes difficult. Hunting birds follow the flocks: a merlin may dash low across the saltings, and a peregrine often watches from a post on the sea wall before stooping into a roost. Short-eared owls quarter the rough grass of the upper marsh by day, hunting voles in the tussocks.

Spring arrives gradually. The days lengthen, the mud warms, and the winter flocks grow restless. Many of the waders begin to moult into breeding plumage before leaving; the knot turn a deep brick red, and the grey plover acquire black faces and bellies edged with white. On still evenings in the early spring the geese rise in long lines and head out to sea, and over a few weeks most of the winter visitors depart. For a short time other travellers pass through, birds that winter far to the south and breed in the far north, stopping on Saltcote for a few days to feed before continuing.

Meanwhile the breeding birds take up their places. Redshank that stayed through the winter move into the middle marsh and nest in tussocks of grass, drawing the stems over the nest to form a hidden bower. Lapwings display over the pastures behind the wall, tumbling through the air with a throbbing wing beat and a wheezing call. Oystercatchers, black and white with bright orange bills, nest on the shingle of the Tiller, and on the open stones above the strand line, ringed plovers lay speckled eggs that are almost impossible to see against the pebbles. Little terns arrive from the south in late spring and form a small, noisy colony on the end of the spit, diving for fish in the shallow channels.

Summer is the quietest season for birds and the most vivid for plants. The sea lavender comes into flower and spreads a purple haze across the middle marsh, and the sea aster follows with pale mauve flowers. Glasswort and cordgrass grow thick and green on the lower ground. In hot spells the salt pans dry out, and the smell of warm mud and drying weed hangs over the creeks. The breeding birds raise their chicks in this period: young redshank and lapwing feed themselves almost from hatching and hide among the grasses when alarmed, while tern chicks wait on the shingle for fish brought by their parents. The highest summer tides sometimes flood the lower nests, and some birds lay again after such losses.

Late in the summer the first returning waders appear, adults that have finished breeding early or failed to raise young. They are still partly in summer plumage, worn and faded. As autumn advances, more and more arrive, and the marsh steadily refills. The glasswort turns red and then purple, the cordgrass yellows, and the plants of the upper marsh die back to brown stems. Autumn gales and high tides scour the creeks and redistribute silt, cutting new channels in some places and raising the mud in others.

I've read it. This one is much more internally consistent than the Aldern document.

## Overview

**Setting.** Saltcote Marsh lies behind the Tiller, a shingle spit that shelters it from the open sea. It is fed by the Wenn and the Callow and flooded twice a day through a gap at the spit's eastern end.

**History.** The area was once a brackish lagoon. Storms cut the spit back, the tide came in more freely, silt built up and the lagoon became saltmarsh. Later a clay sea wall turned the northern margin into pasture.

**Zones, from the bay upward:**
- Mudflats
- Low marsh with cordgrass and glasswort
- Middle marsh with sea lavender, aster and purslane
- Upper marsh with sea couch and rushes
- Salt pans scattered throughout

**Seasons:**
- **Winter:** brent geese, wigeon, teal and waders. The waders split the mud between them by bill length. They roost on high ground at high tide and are hunted by merlin, peregrine and short-eared owl.
- **Spring:** waders moult into breeding plumage (red knot, black-bellied grey plover) and leave, and passage migrants stop briefly. Redshank, lapwing, oystercatcher, ringed plover and little tern settle in to breed.
- **Summer:** sea lavender and aster flower, chicks are raised, and high tides sometimes flood nests, so some birds lay again.
- **Autumn:** worn adults return first, glasswort reddens, and gales reshape the creeks.

## Small points

- **Rivers and the sea wall.** The rivers come from the north, and the sea wall runs along the northern margin. The text doesn't say how they pass through or around the wall, for example by sluices or outfalls.
- **The ending.** It stops at autumn without closing the cycle back into winter. It may be unfinished, or one part of a longer piece.
- **"Wenn."** Your previous document had the Aldern join the "Wenne." That may be a coincidence, but if the two are meant to share a world, you'll want to decide whether these are the same river.
- **Natural history.** This all checks out as far as I can tell: the plumages, nest sites, feeding methods and plant zonation are accurate for a temperate saltmarsh.

What would you like to do with it? I can summarise it, edit it, extend it, or compare it with the Aldern piece.
